tasks.title: Duplicates in linear time
tasks.statement: The function dedupe(items) removes repeats while keeping the order of first occurrences. Right now it is quadratic and does not finish in time on large data. Speed it up (use a set of the items already seen).
tasks.hint: seen = set(); for each x: if x is not in seen, add it to seen and to the result.

tasks.title: The most frequent words
tasks.statement: top_words(words, k) returns the k most frequent words as (word, count) pairs, in descending order of count, ties broken alphabetically. The current version calls words.count for every word and does not finish in time on a large input. Speed it up (collections.Counter).
tasks.hint: Counter(words).items(), then sorted with the key (-count, word) and the slice [:k].

tasks.title: Fibonacci with a cache
tasks.statement: The recursive fib(n) recomputes the same things and does not finish in time even for n = 90. Add caching (functools.cache) without changing the logic.
tasks.hint: from functools import cache and @cache above def fib.

tasks.title: How many numbers in the ranges
tasks.statement: count_in_ranges(nums, queries): nums is a sorted list, queries are (lo, hi) pairs; for each one return how many numbers of nums lie in [lo, hi]. The current version scans the list for every query and is too slow. Use the bisect module.

tasks.title: Maximum in a sliding window
tasks.statement: window_max(nums, k) returns the maximums of all windows of length k. The current version takes max of a slice for every window and is too slow for a large k. Speed it up (a monotonic queue, collections.deque with indexes).
tasks.hint: The deque keeps indexes in decreasing order of values: pop from the end the ones smaller than the new one, from the front the ones that left the window.

tasks.title: Sums on ranges
tasks.statement: The class RangeSum(data) answers queries query(l, r), the sum of data[l:r]. Right now every query recomputes the sum and is too slow with many queries. Prepare prefix sums in __init__ so that a query takes constant time.
tasks.hint: prefix[i] = the sum of the first i elements; the answer is prefix[r] - prefix[l]; itertools.accumulate with an initial 0.

tasks.title: Call counts through cProfile
tasks.statement: Write call_counts(func): run func() under cProfile and return a dict mapping function name to number of calls, only for the functions defined in the same file as func (compare func.__code__.co_filename with the file name in the statistics).
tasks.hint: pr = cProfile.Profile(); pr.runcall(func); stats = pstats.Stats(pr).stats; the keys are (file, line, name), the values are (cc, nc, tt, ct, callers).

tasks.title: Your own timing
tasks.statement: Write bench(func, repeat=5, number=20): using timeit.repeat, run func number times in each of repeat series and return the minimum time of a single call (in seconds, a floating-point number).

tasks.title: Two numbers with a given sum
tasks.statement: two_sum(nums, target): the indexes (i, j), i < j, of two numbers whose sum is target, or None if there is no such pair. The double loop does not finish in time on large data: use a dict mapping value to index and a single pass.
tasks.hint: seen = {}; for each i: need = target - nums[i]; if need is in seen, return (seen[need], i); otherwise seen[nums[i]] = i.
